difficultyReason: Conclusion rests on three conjoined conditions: a constitutional provision, an unambiguous textual meaning, and absence of competing constitutional values. Trap (B) is too broad — it would license overturning statutes whenever any constitutional tension exists. Trap (C) is too narrow — it covers only criminal statutes. Trap (E) inverts the judge's order of priority.
stimulus: Judge: A statute restricting outdoor political canvassing was struck down last week. Some commentators object that judges should defer to legislatures on matters of policy. That concern would have force if the case turned on policy disagreement, but it did not. The statute's language plainly burdened speech, the state's constitution unambiguously protects such speech, and no competing constitutional value was at stake in the dispute. In these circumstances, invalidating the statute was the correct outcome.
questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the judge's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: When a statute's terms on their face restrict an activity that a constitutional provision unambiguously protects, and no competing constitutional value is implicated, a court is justified in invalidating the statute.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Whenever a court perceives tension between a statute and any constitutional value, the court is justified in setting the statute aside.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A criminal statute whose language restricts constitutionally protected activity must be declared void by any court before which it is challenged.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Judges should defer to legislatures on contested questions of policy but not on questions of statutory interpretation.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Where a legislature has weighed competing constitutional values in enacting a statute, courts should uphold the legislature's judgment rather than substitute their own.

explanations.correct: The judge rests the outcome on three stated facts: the statute's plain terms burdened speech, the constitution unambiguously protects such speech, and no competing constitutional value was involved. Principle (A) combines exactly those three conditions and licenses invalidation.
explanations.B: Too broad — licenses invalidation on any perceived tension, which would justify conclusions the judge explicitly refuses to draw when policy disagreement is the real issue.
explanations.C: Too narrow — restricts the rule to criminal statutes, but the canvassing statute need not be criminal, so the principle may not reach this case.
explanations.D: Tangential — the judge accepts deference on policy but the argument is about when invalidation is warranted, not when deference applies.
explanations.E: Reversed — this principle describes a case in which courts should uphold a statute, the opposite of what the judge did.

difficultyReason: Conclusion depends on three conditions: scarce resource, comparable medical prospects between candidates, and one candidate's greater social isolation affecting recovery. Trap (B) omits the comparable-prospects condition. Trap (D) is inverted — it prioritizes social value rather than recovery conditions.
stimulus: Hospital ethicist: Our transplant committee faced two candidates equally matched on the usual medical criteria — compatibility, urgency, and projected graft survival. One lives alone in a remote town with no nearby support network; the other has a large household that can assist with post-operative care. The committee awarded the organ to the second candidate. Some colleagues have called this decision discriminatory. It was not: given the scarcity of donor organs, awarding it where recovery conditions were more favorable was correct.
questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the ethicist's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Patients with strong social networks should always be preferred as transplant recipients because their recovery is more certain.

choices.label: B
choices.text: When a life-saving resource is scarce, it should be awarded to the candidate whose post-treatment circumstances, rather than social worth, render recovery more likely.

choices.label: C
choices.text: When a scarce life-saving resource is at stake and two candidates are medically equivalent, it is permissible to award it to whichever candidate's post-treatment circumstances render successful recovery more probable.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Medical resources should be allocated so as to maximize the total social contribution expected from the recipient's recovery.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No patient should be denied medical treatment on the basis of characteristics unrelated to the diagnosis being treated.

explanations.correct: The ethicist's conclusion rests on three stated conditions: the resource is scarce, the two candidates were medically equivalent, and recovery conditions differ. Principle (C) combines all three and licenses awarding the organ where recovery is more probable.
explanations.A: Too broad — endorses always preferring well-networked patients, even when medical criteria are not equivalent, which the ethicist does not claim.
explanations.B: Too broad — drops the 'medically equivalent' condition and would license overriding medical criteria by recovery conditions, which the ethicist does not do.
explanations.D: Reversed in motivation — the ethicist explicitly disclaims social-worth reasoning, whereas this principle grounds the decision in social contribution.
explanations.E: Tangential — the ethicist is not defending a non-discrimination norm but a tiebreaker rule.

difficultyReason: Conclusion requires three conditions: employee knowledge of wrongdoing, exhaustion of internal channels, and public interest in disclosure. Trap (A) is too broad, omitting internal-exhaustion. Trap (D) aligns with the concession rather than the conclusion.
stimulus: Columnist: A former analyst at a defense contractor released documents showing the firm had falsified safety tests on a component used in commercial aircraft. Her critics emphasize that confidentiality agreements bind employees to silence. That obligation is real, but it is not absolute. The analyst had firsthand knowledge that the falsification was ongoing, she had reported it internally without result, and the public's safety was directly at stake. Her disclosure was therefore justified.
questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the columnist's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An employee who becomes aware of significant wrongdoing by her employer is entitled to disclose that wrongdoing publicly.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Public disclosure of an employer's wrongdoing by an employee is warranted when the employee has direct knowledge of ongoing wrongdoing, has first pursued internal remedies without success, and the wrongdoing endangers the public.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Confidentiality agreements between employers and employees are unenforceable to the extent that they conflict with any interest of the public.

choices.label: D
choices.text: An employee who signs a confidentiality agreement must honor it in every circumstance in which the employer continues to observe its side of the agreement.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Government agencies, rather than private employees, should bear primary responsibility for exposing corporate wrongdoing that endangers the public.

explanations.correct: The columnist justifies disclosure by pointing to three conditions — direct knowledge of ongoing wrongdoing, exhausted internal remedies, and public safety at stake. Principle (B) ties exactly those three into a standard of justified disclosure.
explanations.A: Too broad — would license disclosure on mere awareness, regardless of severity, internal remedies, or public impact.
explanations.C: Too broad — renders confidentiality void for any public interest, a sweeping claim the columnist does not make.
explanations.D: Aligned with the concession rather than the conclusion — the columnist acknowledges the obligation exists but is not defending its absoluteness.
explanations.E: Shifts the subject to which entity should act, not when an employee's disclosure is justified.

difficultyReason: Conclusion requires the conjunction of species endemism, credible threat of extinction, and absence of comparable ecological substitutes. Trap (B) is too broad; trap (C) is too narrow, restricting to charismatic species; trap (E) reverses the priority.
stimulus: Conservation biologist: A coastal wetland slated for a shipping-terminal expansion is the sole habitat of a small fish, the marsh stickleback, which exists nowhere else. Without intervention, the planned dredging will almost certainly drive the species to extinction, and no other local fish fills its role in the food web. The government insists that economic development must take precedence. It must not: halting the expansion is warranted here.
questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the biologist's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: When a planned project would probably eliminate a species endemic to the site and no ecological substitute for that species exists in the local system, halting the project is warranted.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A government may never permit a project that endangers any wildlife, regardless of the project's economic benefits.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Projects that threaten charismatic species should be subjected to stricter review than projects threatening less visible species.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Economic development should be pursued only when it produces gains exceeding the monetary value of the ecosystems it displaces.

choices.label: E
choices.text: When economic development and species protection conflict, the outcome that maximizes long-term public welfare should prevail.

explanations.correct: The biologist's conclusion rests on three conditions: the stickleback is endemic to the site, extinction is likely if the project proceeds, and no ecological substitute exists. Principle (A) combines those exact three conditions and yields the conclusion that halting is warranted.
explanations.B: Too broad — would license halting any project that endangers any wildlife, including species that are not endemic or have substitutes.
explanations.C: Too narrow — restricts the rule to charismatic species; the stickleback need not be charismatic, so the principle may fail to reach this case.
explanations.D: Tangential — introduces a monetary balancing the biologist does not employ.
explanations.E: Reversed — a welfare-maximization rule could license the expansion if its gains are sufficient, which is the opposite of what the biologist concludes.

difficultyReason: Conclusion requires three conditions: data collection outside the disclosed purpose, user reliance on the disclosure, and material use of the data against users. Trap (B) omits reliance; trap (D) aligns with the concession; trap (E) is inverted.
stimulus: Technology ethicist: A fitness-tracking app disclosed in its sign-up flow that heart-rate data would be used to improve training recommendations. Later reporting revealed that the company had been selling the same data to insurers, who used it to raise premiums for some users. The company points out that buried in the full terms-of-service document was a clause permitting secondary data sales. That clause does not exonerate the company: what it did was wrong.
questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the ethicist's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any commercial transfer of personal data to third parties is impermissible unless the user has been individually compensated for the transfer.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A firm that collects personal data acts wrongly when it uses the data for purposes beyond those the user was told about at sign-up, whenever any user is later disadvantaged by that use.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A firm that collects personal data acts wrongly when it uses the data in a manner outside the purpose foregrounded at sign-up, where users reasonably relied on that stated purpose and the subsequent use materially disadvantages them.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Broad consent clauses in terms-of-service documents, once accepted, authorize any subsequent use of the data that falls within their literal wording.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A firm that sells user data is acting wrongly only if the sale violates an explicit statutory prohibition.

explanations.correct: The ethicist rests the judgment on three conditions: use outside the foregrounded sign-up purpose, user reliance on that purpose, and subsequent material disadvantage (higher premiums). Principle (C) ties those three together precisely.
explanations.A: Too broad — would condemn even transfers users had clearly and knowingly authorized, a conclusion the ethicist does not draw.
explanations.B: Too broad — omits the reliance condition, so it would condemn firms even when users were not misled about the primary purpose.
explanations.D: Aligned with the concession — the ethicist acknowledges the clause exists but denies that it exonerates.
explanations.E: Reversed — would exculpate the firm whenever no statute is violated, the opposite of the ethicist's verdict.

difficultyReason: Conclusion requires three conditions: a primary source exists, a later scholar's interpretation is inconsistent with it, and the scholar had access to the source. Trap (A) is too broad. Trap (D) inverts the direction.
stimulus: Historian: A recently reissued textbook claims that Empress Wu's early policy favored the aristocratic clans over the scholar-officials. But the empress's own memoranda from that period — documents long available in published archives consulted by the textbook's author — detail systematic reassignments that consistently advantaged scholar-officials at the clans' expense. The textbook's characterization is unacceptable: it cannot be allowed to stand.
questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the historian's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A historical characterization is unacceptable whenever any historian has raised objections to it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A textbook's characterization of a historical figure should not stand when primary sources accessible to the textbook's author are inconsistent with that characterization.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Historians are obligated to give primary sources greater evidentiary weight than secondary scholarship whenever the two conflict.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Historians should reserve judgment on a characterization until the relevant primary sources have been independently verified.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Characterizations of rulers based solely on their self-authored memoranda are unreliable and should be treated with skepticism.

explanations.correct: The historian rests the verdict on three conditions: a primary source (the memoranda) exists, its content is inconsistent with the textbook's characterization, and the author had access to that source. Principle (B) captures exactly those three conditions.
explanations.A: Too broad — any objection by any historian would suffice, regardless of source access or inconsistency, licensing conclusions the historian does not draw.
explanations.C: Too narrow on audience — speaks about what historians are obligated to do, not when a characterization should fail to stand; it also omits the access condition.
explanations.D: Reverses the direction — counsels reserving judgment rather than rejecting the characterization, whereas the historian issues a definite rejection.
explanations.E: Inverted — the historian is relying on the memoranda as authoritative, not disparaging them.

difficultyReason: Conclusion requires three conditions: tax on a discretionary activity, externalized social cost, and revenue earmarked for harm mitigation. Trap (A) omits earmarking. Trap (D) is aligned with the concession about regressivity. Trap (E) is inverted.
stimulus: Economist: Opponents of the city's new tax on sugary beverages argue that it falls disproportionately on low-income consumers. That regressivity is a real concern, but it does not settle the question. The tax targets a consumption choice that generates documented public-health costs borne by the broader health system, and the revenue is dedicated to clinics serving the same neighborhoods that pay the tax. Under these conditions, enacting the tax was justified.
questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the economist's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A tax on a discretionary consumption choice that imposes demonstrable social costs is justified whenever the tax is projected to reduce the targeted consumption.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A tax targeting a discretionary consumption choice is justified when the activity imposes demonstrable costs on those outside it and the tax revenue is directed to mitigating those costs within the affected communities.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Any policy whose burden falls disproportionately on low-income residents should be rejected in favor of alternatives that distribute costs more evenly.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A tax is justified only if the primary burden falls on those who can most easily absorb it.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A government should avoid taxes whose revenues are earmarked for specific programs rather than flowing into the general treasury.

explanations.correct: The economist justifies the tax on three grounds: the activity is discretionary, imposes external costs on the health system, and the revenue is earmarked to the clinics in the affected communities. Principle (B) ties all three conditions into a justification.
explanations.A: Too broad — omits the earmarking condition the economist invokes and would justify taxes whose revenues are spent elsewhere.
explanations.C: Aligned with the concession — the economist acknowledges regressivity but does not endorse rejection on that ground.
explanations.D: Aligned with the concession and reversed in upshot — would counsel rejecting the tax, which the economist defends.
explanations.E: Reversed — would condemn the earmarking the economist treats as part of the justification.

difficultyReason: Conclusion requires three conditions: documented displacement risk, meaningful consultation failure, and available less-harmful alternative. Trap (B) is too broad, covering any displacement. Trap (D) is too narrow on housing type. Trap (E) is aligned with the concession.
stimulus: Urban planner: The commission approved a luxury tower on the east-side block last month. Supporters stress the housing shortage that motivated the approval. But the block's long-standing residents, who face documented displacement if the project proceeds, were not meaningfully consulted before the vote, and a modified design preserving most of the existing housing was on the table and would have added nearly as many units. Given this, the commission's decision was wrong.
questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the planner's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: When a development decision poses a documented displacement risk to existing residents, those residents must be meaningfully consulted, and a less displacing alternative of comparable benefit exists, approving the decision is wrong.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any urban development project that may displace existing residents should be rejected, regardless of the project's contribution to housing supply.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Planning commissions should prioritize preserving existing housing stock over adding new housing units of any kind.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Approvals of luxury residential towers must always be preceded by a formal vote among the residents of the block to be redeveloped.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Responses to housing shortages should maximize the total number of new units produced within the jurisdiction.

explanations.correct: The planner's verdict combines three stated conditions: documented displacement risk, failure of meaningful consultation, and the availability of a comparably beneficial, less-displacing alternative. Principle (A) combines exactly those three into a wrongness judgment.
explanations.B: Too broad — condemns any displacing project, including ones with full consultation and no alternative, conclusions the planner does not draw.
explanations.C: Too broad and one-sided — would oppose adding new housing even absent displacement or alternatives, which the planner does not endorse.
explanations.D: Too narrow — limited to luxury towers and imposes a procedural rule stricter than the planner's criterion of meaningful consultation.
explanations.E: Aligned with the concession — the planner acknowledges the housing shortage but does not accept unit-maximization as dispositive.

difficultyReason: Conclusion requires three conditions: work commissioned for public display, later discovery of fabricated provenance, and museum knowledge of the fabrication. Trap (B) omits the commissioning condition. Trap (D) is aligned with the concession about aesthetic value.
stimulus: Curator: The Hartwell Museum's 1890 seascape, long admired for its craftsmanship, has been shown to rest on falsified provenance documents: the painting was commissioned specifically for public exhibition on the strength of a fabricated attribution to a celebrated master, and archivists have now confirmed the fabrication. Defenders of the display argue the work remains aesthetically valuable. So it does; but the museum cannot continue to exhibit it as it has.
questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the curator's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A museum that has come to know that a work commissioned for public display was accepted on the basis of falsified provenance must not continue to exhibit the work on the same basis.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any artwork whose provenance is later shown to be falsified must be removed from public view, regardless of the circumstances of its acquisition.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Museums have a duty to correct their provenance records as new archival evidence becomes available.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The aesthetic value of an artwork provides sufficient justification for its continued public display, whatever its provenance.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Falsified attributions should be publicly acknowledged and then disregarded when assessing an artwork's place in a museum's collection.

explanations.correct: The curator's conclusion rests on three conditions: the painting was commissioned specifically for public exhibition, the attribution used to justify that exhibition was fabricated, and the museum now knows this. Principle (A) ties those three into a prohibition on continuing the same exhibition basis.
explanations.B: Too broad — would mandate removal even when the fabrication was unknown or the work was not acquired for public display on that basis.
explanations.C: Too narrow — imposes only a record-correction duty, which leaves the continued display untouched, whereas the curator's conclusion is that the display cannot continue as it has.
explanations.D: Aligned with the concession — the curator accepts aesthetic value but denies it settles the question.
explanations.E: Reverses the force of the fabrication — would permit continued display after a public note, which is exactly what the curator rejects.

difficultyReason: Conclusion requires three conditions: widespread adoption within a speech community, no communication barrier, and consistency with the language's existing grammatical patterns. Trap (B) is too broad. Trap (C) is too narrow on written usage. Trap (E) is inverted.
stimulus: Linguist: Editors at the journal have rejected submissions that use the verb 'to impact' in the sense 'to affect,' on the grounds that the usage is nonstandard. This position is untenable. The usage is now routine among fluent speakers across many dialects, it causes no confusion for readers, and it conforms to the ordinary pattern by which English converts nouns to verbs. The editors' rule should be withdrawn.
questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the linguist's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A proposed usage rule that forbids a form which is widely adopted by fluent speakers, causes no communication difficulty, and follows the language's established patterns should be withdrawn.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any rule that forbids a widely adopted linguistic form should be withdrawn, regardless of whether it causes confusion or fits existing patterns.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Editorial standards governing formal writing should be based exclusively on patterns documented in written, rather than spoken, usage.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Usages that originated as conversions from one part of speech to another should be treated with caution in formal writing until they have been accepted for at least a generation.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The fact that a linguistic form has been widely adopted is by itself insufficient reason to revise standing usage rules about that form.

explanations.correct: The linguist's conclusion combines three conditions: the usage is widespread among fluent speakers, it causes no confusion, and it fits the established noun-to-verb pattern of English. Principle (A) combines exactly those three and licenses withdrawing the rule.
explanations.B: Too broad — would license withdrawal on adoption alone, which could justify withdrawing rules against genuinely confusing or pattern-violating forms, conclusions the linguist does not draw.
explanations.C: Too narrow and tangential — restricts editorial standards to written usage, which would block the linguist's appeal to spoken-language facts.
explanations.D: Reversed — counsels caution against precisely the type of conversion the linguist defends.
explanations.E: Reversed — denies the very inference the linguist draws from widespread adoption together with the other conditions.
